rv.q: The RSC production of Hilary Mantel's Thomas Cromwell novels is a theatrical triumph that transforms dense historical material into riveting drama.
The production achieves something close to miraculous: It makes you feel as if you were watching history unfold in real time.
The result is a pair of plays that are both intellectually stimulating and emotionally satisfying.
What makes this theatrical enterprise so compelling is the way it transforms what could be dusty historical pageantry into intimate, immediate drama.
These are productions of supreme intelligence and sensitivity, which honor both the complexity of Mantel's prose and the craft of theatrical storytelling.
The RSC's magnificent adaptation of Hilary Mantel's novels about Thomas Cromwell arrives on Broadway with most of its power intact, offering a masterclass in ensemble acting.

It's a regular illuminated manuscript up there: quivering rabbits standing in for doomed courtiers; clucking hens supplied by gossipy ladies-in-waiting; and warthogs and goats in the form of odious, snobby lords.
Of course, those fits of pique can land people in the Tower, a sobering reality that closes this absorbing, uncommonly ambitious chronicle on a chilling note.
It is hard not to wish for something deeper from all those hours onstage.
Still, I found myself wondering whether newcomers to the period might guess from the play that anything else important happened while Cromwell was serving as Henry’s marriage counselor.
The immensely talented actors manage to make every backroom deal, courtier spat, and royal tantrum fully enjoyable.
Wolf Hall brings out the best in Broadway, transforming what could have been a stuffy history lesson into riveting theater that makes the Tudor court feel immediate and alive.
The show is shot through with sly parries and juicy jabs.

Miles closely resembles Robert Stack in that vintage TV series “The Untouchables”: He maintains an implacable façade regardless of what he’s thinking, and that Miles rivets our attention for six hours makes his performance a masterclass in minimalist acting.
Nearly two-dozen finely tuned members of the Royal Shakespeare Company deliver admirable performances in this complex historical drama.
The supple performances provided by these and other cast members cannot, however, compensate for plays that impress but don't transport us.
But is it the subtle, engrossing, mysterious masterpiece that Mantel's novels deserved?
But some adaptations simply work better than others.

cn.t: The RSC's six-hour adaptation of Mantel's Tudor novels earns widespread praise for its intelligence, superb ensemble acting, and ability to transform dense historical material into riveting, immediate drama, though some find it slow.

sg.ra: With a 44'10" proscenium and a stage wider than most Broadway houses, Orchestra Center C-G is the only zone where you get the full picture head-on without sacrificing actor-face detail. Spectacle-heavy productions here (BTTF's DeLorean, Mamma Mia! dance numbers) are blocked edge-to-edge, so off-center seats lose pieces even a few rows in.

This is the house's quiet value zone: full center alignment matters more here than proximity does because the auditorium is wider than deep, so row V center still reads front-on. Last orchestra row is short (~6 seats) with unusual legroom per multiple patrons. Tradeoff specific to Winter Garden: the mezzanine overhang starts around row O per published guides, clipping the top of the stage — fine for naturalistic plays, worse for musicals with fly-in sets.

Wide-house penalty hits hardest here: because the auditorium is broader than deep, side-orchestra angles into the stage are sharper than in a typical Broadway house — the further out you sit, the more the upstage far corner disappears. Multiple patrons specifically call out stage-right pillars clipping their view on Salesman; works better for plays where action holds center than for musicals with full-stage choreography.

In a wider-than-deep house the front center mezzanine rescues the seat selection by giving you the one thing center orchestra can't: altitude to take in the full 44'10" proscenium at once. Multiple patrons specifically cite this row range for Mamma Mia! and BTTF over the rear orchestra, and it avoids both the pillar risk on the sides and the mezz overhang clipping rear stalls.

Wide-house geometry pushes the far-left and far-right mezz off at a sharp angle — the stage-opposite corner is the consistent casualty. Reviewers note the speaker stacks on the edge as a recurring blocker, and because the mezz is only ~9 rows deep, distance isn't the killer — angle is. Good option if you're watching a show where the action centers; poor for full-stage choreography.

sg.n: Box Seats (Box B, C, F, G)
sg.ra: The Winter Garden boxes are widely flagged as among the most obstructed in Broadway — the box structure itself blocks significant stage area and the side angle compounds it. Skip at any price.
